topic: The Inscribed Square Problem: Can You Find a Square on Any Loop?
target_audience: Undergraduate students and advanced high school mathematics enthusiasts

sections.title: The Hook: Shapey the Snail’s Trail
sections.content: Introduce the core problem using a relatable scenario. If a snail crawls in a messy, non-self-intersecting loop and returns to the start, can we always find four points on its slime trail that form a perfect square? This introduces the 'Square Peg Problem' (Toeplitz's conjecture) in an intuitive way.
sections.example: An animation of Shapey the Snail leaving a purple wiggly loop. We try to 'drop' a square frame onto the trail until its four corners touch the line.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Jordan Curves
sections.content: Define a Jordan Curve: a plane simple closed curve. Explain that for this problem, the loop doesn't have to be smooth (like a circle) but it cannot cross itself. Visualize this by stretching a rubber band into various 'blob' shapes.
sections.example: Transforming a perfect circle into a jagged, toothy shape to show that topological properties remain even when the geometry looks chaotic.

sections.title: The Strategy: From Square to Rectangle
sections.content: Explain that proving a square exists is hard, but proving a rectangle exists is a classic entry point. We introduce the concept of 'Pairs of Points'. To find a rectangle, we need two pairs of points that share the same midpoint and are of equal length.
sections.example: Visualizing two line segments of equal length crossing at their centers; as they rotate and move, their endpoints always trace a rectangle.

sections.title: The Configuration Space: Mapping Pairs
sections.content: This is the critical transition. Instead of looking at the loop, we create a new 'map'. For every pair of points (A, B) on our loop, we plot a point in 3D space. The height of this point represents the distance between A and B, and its coordinates represent their midpoint.
sections.example: An animation showing two dots moving along the loop, while a corresponding 3D surface (a 'tent' or 'canopy') grows above the loop.

sections.title: Topological Twist: The Möbius Strip
sections.content: Explain that the collection of all unordered pairs of points on a loop mathematically forms a Möbius Strip. This is a profound topological realization. We show how the boundary of this 'pair-space' is the original loop itself.
sections.example: A paper strip being twisted and glued to show that because we don't care which point is 'first' or 'second', the configuration space naturally has only one side.

sections.title: The Conclusion: The Intersection Proof
sections.content: Synthesize the proof. Because a Möbius Strip cannot be mapped into a 3D space with its boundary on a flat plane without self-intersecting, there must be a point where the surface crosses itself. This intersection point represents two different pairs of points with the same midpoint and length—forming our inscribed shape.
sections.example: An animation of a translucent Möbius Strip being pressed down onto a table. Where the surface overlaps itself, a glowing 'square' icon appears back on the original snail trail.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Status
sections.content: Wrap up by stating that while the rectangle problem is solved for all Jordan curves, the 'Square Peg' version is still one of the most famous open problems for 'rough' curves (fractals). Mention applications in robotics and computer vision.
sections.example: A montage showing different mathematicians' names (Vaughan, Stromquist) and a 'Help Wanted' sign over a fractal loop, inviting the students to solve the remaining mystery.
